items.prompt: A team buys a bigger, more powerful machine to replace their single overloaded server. What kind of scaling is this?
choices: Horizontal scaling
Vertical scaling
Load balancing
Sharding
items.explanation: Making one machine bigger (more CPU/RAM) rather than adding more machines is vertical scaling — it increases capacity without changing how many servers handle traffic.
items.reference:
🖥️ Vertical — one machine, bigger
➕ Horizontal — more machines, split traffic

Why: vertical scaling hits a hard ceiling and stays a single point of failure; horizontal scaling grows roughly linearly and survives one machine failing.

items.prompt: Which of these is a real ceiling that vertical scaling eventually hits, but horizontal scaling doesn't?
choices: There's a biggest single machine money can buy, and it's still a single point of failure
It requires a load balancer
It requires shared state
It only works for read-heavy workloads
items.explanation: Horizontal scaling can, in principle, keep adding machines; vertical scaling always runs into 'there is no bigger machine' eventually, and even the biggest single machine remains one single point of failure.
items.reference:
🖥️ Vertical — one machine, bigger
➕ Horizontal — more machines, split traffic

Why: vertical scaling hits a hard ceiling and stays a single point of failure; horizontal scaling grows roughly linearly and survives one machine failing.

items.prompt: What does a load balancer do when one of the servers behind it stops responding to health checks?
choices: Stops sending it new traffic and routes around it
Restarts the failed server automatically
Shuts down all other servers too
Queues all requests until it recovers
items.explanation: A load balancer routes around servers that fail health checks, sending traffic only to the ones still responding — that's what makes one server's failure survivable instead of an outage.
items.reference:
📥 Clients — talk only to the load balancer
⚖️ Load balancer — picks a server per request, routes around unhealthy ones

Why: clients never address a server directly, which is what lets the load balancer add, remove, or fail over servers transparently.

items.prompt: In a load-balanced setup, who does a client actually send its requests to?
choices: The load balancer, which picks a server per request
Whichever server it contacted last time
All servers simultaneously
A randomly assigned server chosen once at login
items.explanation: Clients address the load balancer, not a specific server — that indirection is what lets the load balancer add, remove, or route around servers without clients needing to know or care.
items.reference:
📥 Clients — talk only to the load balancer
⚖️ Load balancer — picks a server per request, routes around unhealthy ones

Why: clients never address a server directly, which is what lets the load balancer add, remove, or fail over servers transparently.

items.prompt: What does it mean for a server to be "stateless" in the sense this unit uses?
choices: It holds nothing request-specific in its own memory that another server would need for that user's next request
It never writes to a database
It has no configuration files
It only serves GET requests
items.explanation: Statelessness here specifically means no server privately holds request-specific data (like a session) that a different server would need to serve the same user's next request.
items.reference:
🧠 Stateful — request data lives only in one server’s memory
🌐 Stateless — request data lives in a shared store every server can reach

Why: a load balancer can send any request to any server only if no server privately holds data another server would need.

items.prompt: A server stores a logged-in user's session only in its own process memory. What kind of server is this?
choices: Stateless
Stateful
Load balanced
Horizontally scaled
items.explanation: Storing session data only in one server's own memory is exactly what makes it stateful — a different server has no way to see that data.
items.reference:
🧠 Stateful — request data lives only in one server’s memory
🌐 Stateless — request data lives in a shared store every server can reach

Why: a load balancer can send any request to any server only if no server privately holds data another server would need.

items.prompt: Why does statelessness matter specifically for horizontal scaling, more than for a single-server setup?
choices: A single server always handles every request from a given user, so private in-memory state never gets exposed as a problem until a second server is added
Stateless servers are always faster
A single server can't store any state at all
Horizontal scaling requires fewer total resources
items.explanation: On one server, every request from a user necessarily lands on that same, only server, so in-memory state 'just works' by accident — the problem only surfaces once a load balancer can send requests to more than one server.
items.reference:
🧠 Stateful — request data lives only in one server’s memory
🌐 Stateless — request data lives in a shared store every server can reach

Why: a load balancer can send any request to any server only if no server privately holds data another server would need.

items.prompt: What does a "sticky session" do?
choices: Routes every request from a given client back to the same server it first used
Stores every session in a shared database
Prevents a load balancer from ever failing over
Compresses session data before sending it
items.explanation: A sticky session pins a client to the specific server it first landed on, usually via a cookie, so all of that client's subsequent requests go back to the same machine.
items.reference:
📌 Sticky session — pins a client to one server, works around statefulness
🗄️ Shared store — removes statefulness, any server can serve any request

Why: sticky sessions keep the data on one server, so that server’s crash still loses it; a shared store survives any one server going down.

items.prompt: Why are sticky sessions described as a workaround rather than a real fix for statefulness?
choices: Because the session data still lives only on one server, which can still lose it if that server goes down
Because they're slower than stateless requests in every case
Because they require a shared database anyway
Because they only work with round robin
items.explanation: Sticky sessions never move the data anywhere shared — they just make sure requests keep finding the one server that has it, so that server's crash still loses the data entirely.
items.reference:
📌 Sticky session — pins a client to one server, works around statefulness
🗄️ Shared store — removes statefulness, any server can serve any request

Why: sticky sessions keep the data on one server, so that server’s crash still loses it; a shared store survives any one server going down.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, what specifically happened after TicketRush added a second server?
choices: 42% of users were randomly logged out mid-checkout
The site became twice as slow
The database ran out of storage
Nothing changed, the fix worked as intended
items.explanation: Adding a second server exposed the in-memory session bug: users whose login landed on one server got treated as logged out when a later request landed on the other.
items.reference:
🖥️ Before — 1 server, CPU pinned at 100%
🔓 After adding a 2nd server — 42% of users randomly logged out

Why: the session lived only in the memory of whichever server created it, so a second server had no way to recognize an existing login.

items.prompt: What was TicketRush's original problem, before the second server was added?
choices: A single server's CPU pinned at 100% during a ticket drop, causing queued requests
Users were being logged out randomly
The load balancer was misconfigured
Sessions were being duplicated across servers
items.explanation: The original problem was pure capacity — one server maxing out its CPU during a traffic spike, not yet anything to do with sessions or multiple servers.
items.reference:
🖥️ Before — 1 server, CPU pinned at 100%
🔓 After adding a 2nd server — 42% of users randomly logged out

Why: the session lived only in the memory of whichever server created it, so a second server had no way to recognize an existing login.

items.prompt: What is a "single point of failure"?
choices: A single component whose failure takes down the entire service
Any server that has ever failed at least once
A load balancer with more than one algorithm configured
A server that handles more traffic than others
items.explanation: A single point of failure is any one component that, if it fails, brings down the whole service — a single server (however powerful) is always one, until there's at least a second one to fail over to.
items.reference:
⚠️ Single point of failure — one component whose failure takes down the whole service
✅ Redundancy — more than one instance, so one failing still leaves the others serving

Why: a single server is always a single point of failure regardless of how big it is — only adding more instances removes that specific risk.

items.prompt: Does making a single server much bigger (vertical scaling) remove it as a single point of failure?
choices: No — it's still the only machine, so its failure still takes down the whole service
Yes — a bigger machine is inherently more reliable
Only if it has redundant power supplies
Yes, as long as it never runs at 100% CPU
items.explanation: Vertical scaling adds capacity, not redundancy — there's still exactly one machine, so it remains a single point of failure no matter how powerful it gets; only adding more instances changes that.
items.reference:
⚠️ Single point of failure — one component whose failure takes down the whole service
✅ Redundancy — more than one instance, so one failing still leaves the others serving

Why: a single server is always a single point of failure regardless of how big it is — only adding more instances removes that specific risk.

items.prompt: With 3 servers A, B, C and plain round robin, what order do the first 5 requests get routed in?
choices: A, B, C, A, B
A, A, B, B, C
Random each time
Whichever server is least busy each time
items.explanation: Round robin cycles through the fixed server order repeatedly — A, B, C, then back to A, B for the 4th and 5th requests.
items.reference:
🔁 Round robin — cycles A, B, C, A, B, C…
⚖️ Best fit — equal-cost requests, equal-capacity servers

Why: round robin ignores both current load and server capacity, so it only distributes fairly when every request and every server are roughly equal.

items.prompt: Under what condition does plain round robin distribute load well?
choices: When requests are roughly equal cost and servers are roughly equal capacity
Only when there are exactly 2 servers
Only when sessions are stateless
Only when health checks are disabled
items.explanation: Round robin's fairness assumption is that every request costs about the same and every server can handle that cost equally — break either assumption and 'equal request counts' stops meaning 'equal load.'
items.reference:
🔁 Round robin — cycles A, B, C, A, B, C…
⚖️ Best fit — equal-cost requests, equal-capacity servers

Why: round robin ignores both current load and server capacity, so it only distributes fairly when every request and every server are roughly equal.

items.prompt: What does a least-connections load balancer use to decide which server gets the next request?
choices: Whichever healthy server currently has the fewest active connections
The server that responded fastest last time
Round-robin order, ignoring load
A fixed weight assigned to each server
items.explanation: Least connections picks whichever server currently has the fewest active (in-flight) connections, reacting to real-time load instead of just a fixed rotation.
items.reference:
📊 Least connections — sends the request to whichever server has fewest active connections right now
🔄 Needs live tracking — a start and a finish signal per request

Why: it reacts to actual current load instead of just request count, but only stays accurate if every request correctly reports when it starts and ends.

items.prompt: For least connections to stay accurate, what does the load balancer need reported for every request?
choices: Both when a request starts and when it finishes
Only when a request starts
Only the total number of requests ever sent
The client's IP address
items.explanation: The active-connection count is only correct if both the start and the completion of each request are reported — missing either one drifts the balancer's view of which server is actually busy.
items.reference:
📊 Least connections — sends the request to whichever server has fewest active connections right now
🔄 Needs live tracking — a start and a finish signal per request

Why: it reacts to actual current load instead of just request count, but only stays accurate if every request correctly reports when it starts and ends.

items.prompt: A request finishes but the code never calls the balancer's "finish" signal for that server. What happens?
choices: The server looks falsely busier than it is and gets starved of new traffic it could actually handle
The server gets marked unhealthy immediately
The load balancer crashes
Nothing — connection counts don't affect routing decisions
items.explanation: A missed 'finish' signal leaves a phantom connection counted against that server forever, making it look busier than it really is and causing the balancer to route new traffic elsewhere even when it has capacity.
items.reference:
📊 Least connections — sends the request to whichever server has fewest active connections right now
🔄 Needs live tracking — a start and a finish signal per request

Why: it reacts to actual current load instead of just request count, but only stays accurate if every request correctly reports when it starts and ends.

items.prompt: A large server has weight 2 and a small server has weight 1 in weighted round robin. Roughly what share of requests does the large server get?
choices: About twice as many as the small server
Exactly the same as the small server
All of them
Half as many as the small server
items.explanation: A weight of 2 versus 1 means the larger server receives roughly twice the share of requests — proportional to its assigned weight, not an equal split.
items.reference:
💪 Weight 2 — gets twice the share of requests
🪶 Weight 1 — gets the baseline share

Why: plain round robin sends every server the same request count regardless of capacity; weights let a bigger server absorb proportionally more.

items.prompt: What has to happen for weighted round robin's weights to stay a good match for reality?
choices: Someone has to set and update them as server capacity actually changes
Nothing — weights are computed automatically from CPU usage
They only need to be set once, ever
They're irrelevant as long as health checks pass
items.explanation: Weights are typically set by a human based on known server capacity — if capacity changes (a bigger machine swapped in, say) and the weight isn't updated, the routing no longer matches reality.
items.reference:
💪 Weight 2 — gets twice the share of requests
🪶 Weight 1 — gets the baseline share

Why: plain round robin sends every server the same request count regardless of capacity; weights let a bigger server absorb proportionally more.

choices: They're lost entirely — there's no other copy of the data anywhere
They automatically fail over to Server B with no data loss
The load balancer restores them from a backup
Nothing — sticky sessions replicate automatically
items.explanation: Sticky sessions don't create a second copy of the data anywhere — they only ensure requests keep finding the one server that has it, so that server's crash takes the sessions with it.
items.reference:
📌 Sticky session — pins a client to one server, works around statefulness
🗄️ Shared store — removes statefulness, any server can serve any request

Why: sticky sessions keep the data on one server, so that server’s crash still loses it; a shared store survives any one server going down.

items.prompt: What does a shared session store change that sticky sessions don't?
choices: It makes servers genuinely interchangeable — any server can serve any user's request
It makes the load balancer unnecessary
It removes the need for health checks
It eliminates network calls entirely
items.explanation: With a shared store, no server needs to be the specific one that created a session — any server can read the same data, which is what makes servers truly interchangeable instead of pinned.

items.prompt: A server is running (the process hasn't crashed) but can't reach its own database. A health check that only opens a TCP connection to the port will report it as:
choices: Healthy — even though it can't actually serve most real requests
Unhealthy — TCP checks always test the database too
It will refuse to answer at all
It will be removed from rotation automatically
items.explanation: A bare TCP/liveness check only confirms the process is listening — it says nothing about whether the server can actually complete a real request, so a server with a broken dependency can pass it and still receive traffic it can't handle.
items.reference:
🩺 Passes — stays in (or rejoins) rotation
❌ Fails — removed from rotation immediately, no new requests routed there

Why: a load balancer that keeps routing to a dead server actively fails every request sent there instead of absorbing the loss into the healthy servers.

items.prompt: What does a load balancer do immediately after a server fails its health check?
choices: Removes it from rotation so no new requests are sent to it
Sends it double the traffic to test recovery
Deletes the server permanently
Waits for a human to intervene before doing anything
items.explanation: Failing a health check gets a server pulled from rotation right away — no new requests are routed there until it starts passing checks again.
items.reference:
🩺 Passes — stays in (or rejoins) rotation
❌ Fails — removed from rotation immediately, no new requests routed there

Why: a load balancer that keeps routing to a dead server actively fails every request sent there instead of absorbing the loss into the healthy servers.

items.prompt: Would switching from round robin to least connections have fixed TicketRush's session bug?
choices: No — the bug was caused by statefulness, not by which algorithm chose the server
Yes — least connections avoids statefulness issues
Yes, but only combined with sticky sessions
No algorithm can ever be combined with a stateless design
items.explanation: Which algorithm picks a server and where that user's session data lives are independent concerns — any algorithm can send a request to a server that doesn't have that user's session if sessions are stored only in-memory.
items.reference:
⚖️ Algorithm choice — affects distribution fairness
🌐 Statelessness — a separate concern, affects correctness

Why: which algorithm routes a request and where that request’s data lives are independent decisions — fixing one doesn’t fix the other.

items.prompt: Two identical servers, similar-cost checkout requests — which algorithm is likely to perform about as well as least connections here?
choices: Round robin — its assumptions (equal cost, equal capacity) are satisfied
Weighted round robin with mismatched weights
No algorithm can work without a shared store
Sticky sessions, since it's the simplest
items.explanation: Round robin performs well exactly when its assumptions hold — equal-cost requests and equal-capacity servers is precisely round robin's best case, so the extra bookkeeping of least connections buys little here.
items.reference:
⚖️ Algorithm choice — affects distribution fairness
🌐 Statelessness — a separate concern, affects correctness

Why: which algorithm routes a request and where that request’s data lives are independent decisions — fixing one doesn’t fix the other.

items.prompt: Implement RoundRobinBalancer.nextServer() so it cycles through servers in order and never returns an unhealthy one.

tests.description: cycles through healthy servers in order
tests.expr: expect((() => { const lb = new RoundRobinBalancer([{ id: "A" }, { id: "B" }]); return [lb.nextServer().id, lb.nextServer().id, lb.nextServer().id]; })()).toEqual(["A", "B", "A"])

tests.description: skips an unhealthy server
tests.expr: expect((() => { const lb = new RoundRobinBalancer([{ id: "A" }, { id: "B" }, { id: "C" }]); lb.markHealth("B", false); return [lb.nextServer().id, lb.nextServer().id, lb.nextServer().id]; })()).toEqual(["A", "C", "A"])

tests.description: throws when no servers are healthy
tests.expr: expect(() => { const lb = new RoundRobinBalancer([{ id: "A" }]); lb.markHealth("A", false); lb.nextServer(); }).toThrow()

items.explanation: Cycling the cursor over the full server list (not just the healthy ones) keeps the rotation predictable as health flips, while the healthy-check inside the loop means an unhealthy server is skipped without ever being returned — and if every server is unhealthy, the loop exhausts and the function throws instead of silently returning a dead server.

Why: round robin ignores both current load and server capacity, so it only distributes fairly when every request and every server are roughly equal.

items.prompt: Implement LeastConnectionsBalancer's nextServer, startRequest, and finishRequest so it always routes to the healthy server with fewest active connections.

tests.description: picks the server with fewer active connections
tests.expr: expect((() => { const lb = new LeastConnectionsBalancer([{ id: "A" }, { id: "B" }]); lb.startRequest("A"); return lb.nextServer().id; })()).toBe("B")

tests.description: finishRequest frees up a server to be picked again
tests.expr: expect((() => { const lb = new LeastConnectionsBalancer([{ id: "A" }, { id: "B" }]); lb.startRequest("A"); lb.startRequest("B"); lb.finishRequest("A"); return lb.nextServer().id; })()).toBe("A")

tests.description: ties go to the first server in the list
tests.expr: expect((() => { const lb = new LeastConnectionsBalancer([{ id: "A" }, { id: "B" }]); return lb.nextServer().id; })()).toBe("A")

items.explanation: nextServer() has to look only at currently healthy servers and pick the minimum activeConnections among them; startRequest/finishRequest keep that count accurate by incrementing when work is assigned and decrementing (clamped at 0) when it completes — without both halves being called correctly, the count drifts and the balancer's picture of 'who's busy' stops matching reality.

items.prompt: Implement HealthAwarePool.recordHealthCheck and healthyIds so a failed check immediately removes a server from the healthy set.

tests.description: all servers healthy initially
tests.expr: expect(new HealthAwarePool(["A", "B", "C"]).healthyIds()).toEqual(["A", "B", "C"])

tests.description: a failed check removes the server from healthyIds
tests.expr: expect((() => { const p = new HealthAwarePool(["A", "B"]); p.recordHealthCheck("A", false); return p.healthyIds(); })()).toEqual(["B"])

tests.description: a later passing check re-adds the server
tests.expr: expect((() => { const p = new HealthAwarePool(["A", "B"]); p.recordHealthCheck("A", false); p.recordHealthCheck("A", true); return p.healthyIds(); })()).toEqual(["A", "B"])

items.explanation: recordHealthCheck just flips the matching server's healthy flag to whatever the check reported (true on pass, false on fail); healthyIds() then filters down to only the servers currently marked healthy — this is the piece a load balancer's nextServer() relies on to skip a server the instant it starts failing checks, without waiting for a human to intervene.

tests.expr: expect((() => { const p = new HealthAwarePool(["A"]); p.recordHealthCheck("Z", false); return p.healthyIds(); })()).toEqual(["A"])

items.explanation: recordHealthCheck just flips the matching server's healthy flag to whatever the check reported (true on pass, false on fail); healthyIds() then filters down to only the servers currently marked healthy — this is the piece a load balancer's nextServer() relies on to skip a server the instant it starts failing checks, without waiting for a human to intervene.
items.reference:
🩺 Passes — stays in (or rejoins) rotation
❌ Fails — removed from rotation immediately, no new requests routed there

Why: a load balancer that keeps routing to a dead server actively fails every request sent there instead of absorbing the loss into the healthy servers.

items.prompt: Implement SharedSessionStore's create, read, and destroy methods.

tests.description: create then read returns the same userId
tests.expr: expect((() => { const store = new SharedSessionStore(); const id = store.create("user-1"); return store.read(id).userId; })()).toBe("user-1")

tests.description: reading an unknown sessionId returns null
tests.expr: expect(new SharedSessionStore().read("nope")).toBe(null)

tests.description: destroy removes the session so it reads back as null
tests.expr: expect((() => { const store = new SharedSessionStore(); const id = store.create("user-1"); store.destroy(id); return store.read(id); })()).toBe(null)

items.explanation: create() has to store the session under a key it also returns, so a caller (any server) can later read it back by that same id; read() must return null rather than throw for a missing/destroyed session, since 'not logged in' is an expected, normal outcome, not an error — this is exactly what lets a different server than the one that ran create() successfully read the session back.
items.reference:
🧠 Stateful — request data lives only in one server’s memory
🌐 Stateless — request data lives in a shared store every server can reach

Why: a load balancer can send any request to any server only if no server privately holds data another server would need.

items.prompt: Implement WeightedRoundRobinBalancer.buildSequence() so each server appears `weight` times, interleaved evenly.

tests.description: weight 2 appears twice as often as weight 1 across the sequence
tests.expr: expect((() => { const lb = new WeightedRoundRobinBalancer([{ id: "A", weight: 2 }, { id: "B", weight: 1 }]); const seq = lb.buildSequence(); return [seq.filter((id) => id === "A").length, seq.filter((id) => id === "B").length]; })()).toEqual([2, 1])

tests.description: equal weights produce equal counts
tests.expr: expect((() => { const lb = new WeightedRoundRobinBalancer([{ id: "A", weight: 1 }, { id: "B", weight: 1 }]); return lb.buildSequence().length; })()).toBe(2)

tests.description: an unhealthy server contributes nothing to the sequence
tests.expr: expect((() => { const lb = new WeightedRoundRobinBalancer([{ id: "A", weight: 3 }, { id: "B", weight: 1 }]); lb.markHealth("A", false); return lb.buildSequence(); })()).toEqual(["B"])

items.explanation: Building the sequence round-by-round (one pass per server that still has weight left, up to the largest weight in the pool) interleaves higher-weight servers evenly through the sequence instead of bunching all of one server's turns at the start — which matters in practice because a real load balancer draws from this sequence continuously, and a bunched sequence would send a burst of consecutive requests to one server instead of spreading them out.
items.reference:
💪 Weight 2 — gets twice the share of requests
🪶 Weight 1 — gets the baseline share

Why: plain round robin sends every server the same request count regardless of capacity; weights let a bigger server absorb proportionally more.
